doc.title: John Budd interviewed by Monk Rowe, Aspen, Colorado, October 11, 1997 [transcript only]

title: Surgical teams in England and Normandy
summary: How the auxiliary surgical teams worked near the front, twelve-hour shifts, and the courage of young soldiers.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Yes. We went to England and lived in Evesham England for a while until June of 1943 we went to Normandy, to Utah Beach, a few days after it fell we went in the woods there, we went to a hospitals, field hospitals, evacuations hospitals, occasionally battalion aide stations, they were near the front, so they could get patients quickly. And the teams that we had, there were four neurosurgeon teams and there were about 30 general surgical teams, four thoracic surgical teams, four maxillo-facial surgical teams, and six orthopedic teams. We’d always be the same: the chief, the assistant, the anesthetist, two corpsmen and a nurse. And we always worked together, and different hospitals. You’d go and they’d put you in a truck with your equipment and go to some hospital, the front has © Hamilton College Jazz Archive -14-

advanced so go up so you’re near them, and check in to the chief and he’d put you to work. We’d work 12 hour shifts. You’d do 12 noon to 12 midnight, and another team would take on the other hours, and it was a marvelous experience, and you just saw some awful things happen and I just think about those young kids, 19, 20, 21 year olds with terrible things happen to them, and the courage of those guys. It was nothing for us, we weren’t in any danger I don’t think. We had a red cross on our helmet and on our tents and everything like that and if there was any strafing of an area around there, I’m sure the Generals would avoid strafing a hospital area unless by accident. One time there was a lot of it going along at that time and my chief, the guy that was with me, said “do you think we ought to get under the table?” You’re just kidding I’m sure. But we decided no, the patient can’t join us so we’d better stay. Nothing happened though. We never had any trouble.
